question:
A 12-year-old boy who recently immigrated from Namibia is being evaluated for exertional shortness of breath and joint pain for the past month. His mother reports that he used to play soccer but now is unable to finish a game before he runs out of air or begins to complain of knee pain. He was a good student but his grades have recently been declining over the past few months. The mother recalls that he had a sore throat and didn’t go to school for 3 days a few months ago. He had chickenpox at the age of 5 and suffers from recurrent rhinitis. He is currently taking over-the-counter multivitamins. His blood pressure is 110/90 mm Hg, pulse rate is 55/min, and respiratory rate is 12/min. On physical examination, subcutaneous nodules are noted on his elbows bilaterally. On cardiac auscultation, a holosystolic murmur is heard over the mitral area that is localized. Lab work shows:
Hemoglobin 12.9 g/dL
Hematocrit 37.7%
Leukocyte count 5,500/mm3
Neutrophils 65%
Lymphocytes 30%
Monocytes 5%
Mean corpuscular volume 82.2 fL
Platelet count 139,000/mm3
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 35 mm/h
C-reactive protein 14 mg/dL
Antistreptolysin O (ASO) 400 IU (normal range: > 200 IU)
Which is the mechanism behind the cause of this boy’s symptoms?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Streptococcal infection -> Immune response -> Production of antibodies -> Elevated ASO titer -> Type II hypersensitivity reaction -> Tissue damage -> Symptoms in the boy -> Type II hypersensitivity reaction -> 80%
CHAIN: Streptococcal infection -> Immune response -> Immune complex formation -> Deposition in tissues -> Inflammation -> Symptoms in the boy -> Type III hypersensitivity reaction -> 75%
enhanced_information: The boy's symptoms are likely due to a Type II hypersensitivity reaction. Streptococcal infection triggered an immune response leading to the production of antibodies, resulting in an elevated ASO titer. These antibodies cause tissue damage, explaining the symptoms observed in the boy. The evidence paths support the formation of antigen-antibody complexes, which can lead to tissue inflammation and damage, aligning with a Type II hypersensitivity reaction.
analysis: The boy's symptoms, including exertional shortness of breath, joint pain, subcutaneous nodules, and elevated ASO titer, are indicative of rheumatic fever, which is a Type II hypersensitivity reaction triggered by a streptococcal infection. Antibodies produced in response to the infection cross-react with self-antigens, leading to tissue damage and the observed clinical manifestations. This aligns with the enhanced information provided, supporting a Type II hypersensitivity reaction as the underlying mechanism.
